For many computer vision tasks, neural networks can be trained to produce a
low average error, yet they still fail on seemingly simple scenes. Reducing
these failures requires first finding them, but they may not be in a fixed dataset.
We study procedural adversarial learning (PAL), a framework of minimax train-
ing and adversarial evaluation which searches the input space of a procedural
generator for difficult instances. The procedural generator is an interpretable
program mapping a low-dimensional vector of control parameters (e.g. layout,
lighting, pose) to a rendered image and its label. We introduce the Simple-
PAT algorithm, which uses zeroth-order optimization in the procedural gener-
ator's parameter space to propose adversarial training samples that are gener-
ated on demand. We also create PAL-Dojo, a collection of efficient procedu-
ral generators for surface normal

We propose Simple-PAT, a simple algorithm for procedural adversarial training using adversaries
that attack via zeroth-order optimization. Simple-PAT consists of a learner that trains the model
through minibatch gradient descent and an adversary that uses Covariance Matrix Adaptation Evo-
lution Strategy (CMA-ES) Hansen & Ostermeier (2001) to search on procedural controls to generate
the next minibatch based on existing cases the model finds challenging.
To analyze PAT algorithms, we develop PAL-Dojo, a suite of procedural generators for three vision
tasks: surface normal estimation, human pose estimation, and image segmentation. We design these

evidence.excerpt:
Our primary evaluation, procedural adversarial evaluation (PAE), is a worst-case search against each
network after it has completed training; we describe this in the following subsections. The true worst
case cannot be computed with a finite number of queries, so we use best-effort adversaries that probe
each model as a black box subject to a compute budget, and we refer to the worst case an adversary
finds as theevaluation worst case. We consider two PAE adversaries: a single-model adversary
that searches against each model separately, and a cross-model adversary that pools the worst cases
found across models. We also evaluate every model on the same test set of 65,536 scenes sampled
uniformly at random.

evidence.excerpt:
Our single-model evaluation protocol uses a black-box optimizer to search for the procedural pa-
rameters that produce the worst loss for a given network. We use a budget of 2 million queries,
which represents39%of the overall training budget of 5.12 million samples. We split this between
1 million samples of a DIRECT-L search (Gablonsky & Kelley, 2001) and 1 million samples of a
CMA-ES search. This CMA-ES search differs from the search performed during training in several
important ways: (1) it uses a population size of 512 instead of 28 (2) it updates a full covariance
matrix instead of a diagonal parameterization (3) IPOP restarts are permitted (4) the objective is
stationary, allowing for better convergence (Hansen et al., 2019). Combined, these settings give the
evaluation a substantially more powerful search than training.

evidence.excerpt:
For our cross-model evaluation, we pool the worst cases across training seeds and training proce-
dures. We evaluate each network on the worst cases found by the black-box optimizer against other
networks. We report the overall worst loss among the single-model evaluation and the evaluation
on other networks' worst cases. In our experiments, we have five methods and 5 seeds per method.
Thus, the cross-model evaluation has a total of 50M queries, though each model is still only queried
2M times.

In Figure 5 we compare the single-model evaluation and cross-model evaluation. Since the cross-
model evaluation pools the worst cases, it reports errors greater than or equal to the single-model
evaluation. On normals, the two evaluations nearly agree, with the cross-model adversary increasing
the worst case by at most5%for every method. On pose and chair-simple, the increase is at most

evaluation_independence.corroboration_summary: The evaluation adversary uses a substantially more powerful search configuration than training, and the fixed 65,536-scene uniform test set provides an additional measurement outside the training optimization loop.
evaluation_independence.final_evaluation_signal: Worst-case ground-truth task loss discovered by post-hoc black-box search using DIRECT-L and full-covariance CMA-ES with IPOP restarts, pooled across models for the cross-model adversary, plus fixed uniform test-set metrics.
evaluation_independence.optimization_signal: Minibatch forward loss on candidate parameter vectors proposed by internal zeroth-order CMA-ES instances during training.

primary.claim_evidence_alignment: Reported claims of substantial reductions in worst-case error across all four tasks are directly backed by quantitative experimental results and significance tests.
primary.evaluation_assessment: Evaluation includes both single-model and cross-model black-box adversarial searches up to 50M total queries, comparing Simple-PAT against standard uniform training and robust objectives (CVaR, Tilted ERM) across multiple seeds with statistical significance testing.

evaluation_independence.corroboration_summary: Models were evaluated using a separate test set of 65,536 uniformly sampled scenes and cross-model adversarial transfers generated from distinct optimization budgets and architectures.
evaluation_independence.final_evaluation_signal: Worst-case ground-truth task loss (angular error, BCE, MPJPE) discovered by an independent post-hoc black-box search (DIRECT-L and full-covariance CMA-ES with IPOP restarts across 50M cross-model queries) as well as fixed uniform test set metrics.
evaluation_independence.optimization_signal: Minibatch forward loss evaluated on candidate parameter vectors proposed by internal zeroth-order CMA-ES instances during training.

primary.limitations: The authors acknowledge that black-box searches can miss difficult cases in higher-dimensional procedural spaces (such as Chair-Full) and examine discrepancies between single-model and cross-model adversarial evaluations.
primary.method_assessment: The methodology is thoroughly detailed, describing the procedural generators, parameter dimensionality, and the Simple-PAT training algorithm that combines uniform sampling and zeroth-order CMA-ES search with periodic restarts.
primary.quality_rationale: The study presents a clear, well-scoped framework supported by rigorous algorithmic formulations, comprehensive empirical baselines, appropriate ablation and baseline comparisons, and honest disclosure of evaluation limits.
primary.scoped_contribution: The paper introduces procedural adversarial learning (PAL), proposing Simple-PAT—an adversarial training method using CMA-ES over procedural parameter spaces—and PAL-Dojo, a benchmark suite of procedural generators across surface normal estimation, object segmentation, and human pose estimation.

scholarly_quality.rationale: The study presents a clear, well-scoped framework supported by rigorous algorithmic formulations, comprehensive empirical baselines, appropriate ablation and baseline comparisons, and honest disclosure of evaluation limits.
scholarly_quality.uncertainty: The authors acknowledge that black-box searches can miss difficult cases in higher-dimensional procedural spaces (such as Chair-Full) and examine discrepancies between single-model and cross-model adversarial evaluations.

limitations_or_uncertainty.value: Structured research-card claims use title, abstract/summary, metadata, screening rules, and curation. A separate scholarly-quality assessment used bounded full-text excerpts, but unsupported claim, method, or evidence fields remain unextracted.
